Course 22

Ageing well

What changes and what does not in the mind with age, how to look after memory, mood and relationships, and when to seek help.

Lesson 2. Memory over the years

1 · Lesson

With age it is normal to process information somewhat more slowly, to find it harder to recall names or the exact word, and to need more effort to attend to several things at once. This does not stop daily life.

Other abilities hold steady or improve: vocabulary, knowledge, procedural memory (how things are done) and, in many cases, practical judgement. Memory of important distant events is usually well preserved.

Dementia is not a normal part of ageing. It is a decline that affects independence in daily life. Signs worth checking: repeatedly forgetting recent events, getting lost in familiar places, difficulty managing money or medication, or changes in character. When in doubt, the family doctor is the first step; some causes of forgetfulness are treatable.

2 · Example

Forgetting where you left your keys is common at any age. Finding your keys and not knowing what they are for is something else. The difference lies in whether the lapse is occasional and recoverable, or affects the use and meaning of things.

3 · Activity

Talk to an older person you know and ask what they find easier and harder than twenty years ago. Note their answers and compare them with this lesson.
